system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 2 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2151-06-13 17:44:00 to 2151-06-14 18:25:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted for evaluation of a rash, eye irritation, and sore throat following an allogeneic stem cell transplant for CML in myeloblastic crisis. Initial workup ruled out viral infections, and a skin biopsy confirmed chronic graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) affecting the skin and eyes. Oral lesions suggestive of herpes simplex virus were treated with a 7-day course of valacyclovir. Symptoms improved with increased prednisone, higher-dose tacrolimus, and topical therapies for the skin and eyes. Transaminitis was noted but trended downward, likely related to GVHD or medication effects. Abdominal pain was chronic and unchanged, with a normal CT abdomen. The patient stabilized, symptoms resolved, and she was discharged home with updated immunosuppressive and supportive therapies.
problems: Herpes simplex with other specified complications
Nonspecific elevation of levels of transaminase or lactic acid dehydrogenase [LDH]

radiology_notes.text:
INDICATION:  ___ woman with AML status post BMT, c/b GVHD, on chronic
steroids, now presenting with nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain and chills.  To
evaluate for intra-abdominal infection.

COMPARISON:  CT of the abdomen and pelvis ___.

TECHNIQUE:  MDCT images were acquired through the abdomen and pelvis from the
level of the lung bases to the proximal femora after administration of oral
and intravenous contrast.  Sagittal and coronal reformats were generated and
reviewed.

CT OF THE ABDOMEN WITH CONTRAST:  The lung bases appear normal without
evidence of focal consolidation, suspicious nodules or pleural effusions.  The
visualized portion of the heart and pericardium appear unremarkable. 
Previously noted calcified left mediastinal lymph nodes are unchanged.

The liver shows homogeneous attenuation without focal liver lesions.  The
patient is status post cholecystectomy.  There is no intra- or extra-hepatic
biliary dilatation.  Both adrenal glands appear unremarkable.  There is
diffuse fatty infiltration of the pancreas.  A punctate calcification is noted
in the superior aspect of the spleen (2:13) and this along with the calcified
mediastinal lymph nodes suggest prior granulomatous disease.  Both kidneys
show symmetric opacification and excretion of contrast.  4-mm hypodensity in
the upper pole of the right kidney, is too small to characterize, unchanged
since the prior study.  There is no evidence of hydronephrosis or focal renal
lesions.  The stomach, small bowel, and the large bowel appear normal, without
obstruction, wall thickening, or masses.  No significant retroperitoneal or
mesenteric lymphadenopathy is detected.  The aorta is normal in course and
caliber.  There is no intraperitoneal free fluid or air.

CT OF THE PELVIS WITH CONTRAST:  The bladder is partially distended and
appears unremarkable.  The uterus and adnexa are normal.  The sigmoid colon
and rectum are within normal limits.  There is no free fluid or significant
pelvic lymphadenopathy.

OSSEOUS STRUCTURES AND SOFT TISSUES:  No suspicious lytic or sclerotic bone
lesion is detected.

IMPRESSION:

1.  No acute intra-abdominal pathology detected.

2.  Calcified mediastinal lymph nodes and focal calcification in the spleen,
likely relate to prior exposure to granulomatous disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve been feeling really nauseous, especially when I eat or drink. I threw up once last night. And I have this sharp pain in my upper belly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. How long has this been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s been getting worse over the last two days. I’ve been trying lorazepam like I usually do, but it’s not helping this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Any fever, blood in your vomit, or diarrhea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No blood, no diarrhea. I’ve had chills, but my temperature hasn’t gone above 97.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I also see from your clinic visit earlier that there was a mix-up with your medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I was taking three fluconazole pills and only one prednisone. I thought the pills looked different. I didn’t realize I had it backwards.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. You’re supposed to take more prednisone and just one fluconazole. That mistake may have made your graft-versus-host disease harder to control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no. Is that why I’m feeling so sick?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be part of it. We’ve restarted your prednisone at the right dose—60 mg daily. But the high dose of steroids can also irritate your stomach, which might explain the nausea and pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s the medicine helping me but also making me feel worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’re going to treat the stomach irritation while keeping your immune system under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll increase your pantoprazole to twice a day and start a new medication called sucralfate. It coats the stomach to help heal the irritation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds good. Will I need any tests?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll do a CT scan of your abdomen to make sure there’s nothing else going on, like an infection or blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright, I’m glad we’re checking everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. Your CT scan came back. Good news—it shows no signs of infection, blockage, or other problems in your abdomen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. So it’s really just the stomach irritation?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. The scan was completely normal. Your symptoms are most likely due to gastritis from the increased steroid dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the chills? Are those related too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They could be. Sometimes nausea and discomfort can make you feel chilled, even without a fever. We’re not seeing signs of infection in your labs either.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I just reviewed your labs from this morning. Your liver enzymes are a bit high, but they’re at your usual baseline. We think that’s related to your GVHD, not a new problem.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So nothing new to worry about?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at all. Your tacrolimus level is good, and your blood counts are stable. You’re responding well to the treatment for your stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I do feel a little better. The nausea isn’t as bad this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. We’ll keep you on the sucralfate and higher-dose pantoprazole to let your stomach heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my prednisone? Will I stay on 60 mg?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep it at 60 mg for now to control your GVHD, but we’ll watch for side effects. We’ll also make sure you and your husband understand all your medications before you go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, please. I don’t want to make that mistake again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll go over them together. We also adjusted your oxycodone—now it’s 20 mg twice a day for your hip pain, which should be enough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s fine. My hip pain is chronic, and that dose usually works.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. I just got the final report from your CT scan. It confirms no acute issues in your abdomen. The spleen and lymph nodes show old changes, likely from past infections, but nothing active.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Like TB? Because I had the BCG vaccine years ago.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. The calcifications are consistent with that. No treatment needed—it’s just a reminder of your history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you today. Your symptoms have improved, and everything looks stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What changes should I expect with my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll start sucralfate four times a day, take pantoprazole twice daily, and stay on prednisone at 60 mg for now. We’ll taper it later. Oxycodone is now 20 mg twice a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see your oncologist soon. They’ll help manage your prednisone taper and GVHD. Call if nausea returns or you have new symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel much better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’re glad we could help. Take care, and follow those instructions closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—your liver tests are still a bit high, but we believe it’s due to GVHD, not a new issue. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I understand. I’ll keep up with my appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’re doing well. We’ll get your discharge papers ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. I’m ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll have a nurse go over your medications one more time with you and your husband before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, please. I want to make sure I get it right this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. Safety first. We’re here to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll see you in follow-up, but call sooner if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, and get some rest at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted for nausea, vomiting, and epigastric abdominal pain following a medication error in which she mistakenly took fluconazole instead of prednisone. This led to under-treatment of her chronic graft-versus-host disease, requiring re-initiation of high-dose prednisone. The increase in steroids likely worsened steroid-induced gastritis, causing her symptoms. A CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis showed no acute pathology. She was treated with increased pantoprazole and initiation of sucralfate, with symptom improvement. Her transaminitis remained at baseline and was attributed to GVHD. Chronic hip pain was managed with oxycodone. Medication reconciliation was completed with patient and family education. She stabilized and was discharged home with updated medication instructions and follow-up plans.
